extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and advanced students interested in geometry of conics and quadrics
extracted.subtask_description: Classification and analytic study of surfaces of the second degree (quadrics) and detailed properties of the ellipse (parametrization, chords, conjugate diameters, inscribed/circumscribed polygons), including methods to find tangent planes and loci of centres.

rubrics_metrics.name: General fact: six series of circular sections
rubrics_metrics.description: In general every surface of the second degree has six series of circular sections (real or imaginary) parallel to the three principal axes of the surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The positions of the planes of the circular sections are independent of the coefficients D, E, F and the absolute term G of the general quadratic equation. Use the principal axes reduction to determine which of these six series are real or imaginary for a given quadric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case I — Ellipsoid: real circular sections
rubrics_metrics.description: For an ellipsoid referred to its principal axes (A x^2 + B y^2 + C z^2 = 1 with A, B, C > 0 and A < B < C), two series of real circular sections occur; the other series are imaginary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The real circular sections are parallel to the axis of y (or the mean axis of the ellipsoid) when the indicated characteristic equations are real; check the sign/order of A, B, C to determine which series are real.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case II — Hyperboloid of one sheet: two real circular series
rubrics_metrics.description: For a one-sheet hyperboloid reduced to principal axes (one of A, B, C negative; here C negative and A < B), there are only two series of real circular sections, both parallel to the greater axis of the principal elliptic section (the greater real axis of the surface).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solve the characteristic equations derived from the principal-axis form to see which series yield real roots; the other series will be imaginary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case III — Hyperboloid of two sheets: two real circular series
rubrics_metrics.description: For a two-sheet hyperboloid (principal form with one coefficient negative appropriately, e.g., B < C in the reduced form) there are two series of real circular sections; the other series are imaginary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The real circular sections lie in planes parallel to the specified principal axis (here the axis of y or the greater imaginary axis); check sign relations of coefficients to decide which characteristic equations are real.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case IV — Elliptic paraboloid: two real circular series
rubrics_metrics.description: An elliptic paraboloid reduced with axis as z (A = 0) has two series of circular sections (if B < C), both parallel to the axis which lies in the plane of the principal parabolic section whose parameter is the greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other characteristic series are imaginary. Use the reduced paraboloid equation and solve the characteristic conditions to find the planes of circular sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case V — Hyperbolic paraboloid: degenerating circles
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyperbolic paraboloid (principal axes chosen suitably) nominally indicates two series of circular sections parallel to the principal axis, but in this case each 'circle' degenerates into a straight line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminate variables from the system of intersection equations to show the intersection projects as straight lines; i.e., check degeneracy by elimination — the intersection is a straight line rather than a true circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case VI — Cone: two real circular series
rubrics_metrics.description: A quadratic cone referred to principal axes (A x^2 + B y^2 − C z^2 = 0) has two series of circular sections (for A < B), parallel to the axis of x (or to the greater axis of the surface); other series are imaginary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceed via the characteristic equations from the principal-axis form; verify which yield real solutions to identify real circular-section planes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case VII — Elliptic cylinder: two real circular series
rubrics_metrics.description: An elliptic cylinder (reduced to A x^2 + B y^2 = 1) has two series of circular sections parallel to the greater axis of the principal section when A < B; the other characteristic series are imaginary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cylinder’s axis choice simplifies the analysis — apply the same characteristic-equation method to identify the real circular-series directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case VIII — Hyperbolic cylinder: degenerate circles
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyperbolic cylinder suggests two series of circular sections from the characteristic equations, but these circles degenerate into straight lines (as with the hyperbolic paraboloid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show degeneracy by elimination similar to Case V: projected intersections on coordinate planes are straight lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case IX — Parabolic cylinder: degenerate circular sections
rubrics_metrics.description: A parabolic cylinder reduced to form By^2 − a x = 1 has the property that every section by a plane perpendicular to the axis may algebraically appear as a circle, but the circle degenerates into a straight line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the intersection equations to observe the degeneracy into straight lines in the projected intersections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface of revolution condition (when circular-section planes are perpendicular to axis)
rubrics_metrics.description: If certain mixed-coefficient parameters vanish (a = a' = β = β' = 0 and the characteristic reductions give B = A with γ, γ' arbitrary), the surface must be a surface of revolution; the planes of circular section are perpendicular to the axis of revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent patterns of zeroing the off-diagonal/interaction parameters produce the same result (several symmetric choices given). Check the coefficient equalities A = B = C under further vanishing for spheres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sphere condition (all planes indeterminate)
rubrics_metrics.description: If additionally γ = γ' = 0, then A = B = C and the surface is a sphere; the planes of circular section are indeterminate (every central plane orthogonal to any diameter gives circular sections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the sphere as the fully symmetric special case when all principal coefficients equal and all cross/linear coefficients vanish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangency of coordinate planes — trace conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Coordinate planes are tangential to a quadratic surface when each trace (the curve obtained by setting one coordinate = 0) denotes a point, a line, or two lines. The necessary conditions are determinant-like relations among the trace-coefficients (displayed as equations analogous to (5), (6), (7)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the conic-section criteria for degeneracy of a quadratic in two variables (vanishing discriminant-like combinations) — the paper gives explicit algebraic combinations to test whether a trace is a point or line and then eliminates parameters to get relations between remaining coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: General equation referred to three tangent planes
rubrics_metrics.description: When a quadric is referred to three tangent planes as coordinate planes, the equation takes a specific expanded form with coefficients expressed by rational expressions in the tangent-plane coefficients (the paper presents the full expression and relations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitute the plane equations and use the trace-degeneracy conditions to derive the general form; the provided large-form expression gives the mapping from tangent-plane parameters to the quadric coefficients — use the sign choice as noted ('employ the negative sign' if substitution does not produce a valid quadric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Centres of inscribed and circumscribed quadrics in a parallelepiped coincide
rubrics_metrics.description: If surfaces of the second order are inscribed in a given parallelepiped and others are circumscribed about the same parallelepiped, all these inscribed and circumscribed surfaces have the same centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer the parallelepiped faces as coordinate planes and use the derived relations (12–20) between the quadric coefficients and the parallelepiped-face parameters; the algebraic elimination shows the same centre X, Y, Z results for all such surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipse parametrization by eccentric anomaly
rubrics_metrics.description: Parametrize ellipse by x = a cos φ, y = b sin φ (eccentric anomaly φ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This parametrization (introducing eccentric anomaly) is recommended as it simplifies many investigations of ellipse properties — chords, tangents, conjugate diameters, areas, and polygon constructions are all neatly expressed via φ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chord equation in terms of eccentric anomalies
rubrics_metrics.description: Equation of chord joining P1(φ1) and P2(φ2) on the ellipse can be written compactly in trig form (given as equation (2) in the paper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the parametric cos/sin forms to express chord equation and deduce middle-point coordinates and the radius bisecting the chord; this also yields chord length formula (equation (3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugate diameters — eccentric-anomaly relation and construction
rubrics_metrics.description: If OP and OP' are conjugate radii (diameters), their eccentric anomalies satisfy tan φ' = −cot φ so that φ' = φ ± π/2, giving two conjugate points to any given point; a geometric construction via the auxiliary circle produces the conjugate diameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: from point P on ellipse draw perpendicular to major axis to meet circle at Q, draw Q'O perpendicular to QO, etc., as described — yields conjugate point P' and diameter OP'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area/sector and segment scaling between ellipse and auxiliary circle
rubrics_metrics.description: An elemental sector/triangle/segment of the ellipse corresponds to a scaled element of the auxiliary circle: ratios of triangle PiOPj, sector P1OP2 and segment upon P1P2 to their circle-counterparts are each equal to b/a (minor/major axis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the parametric mapping between circle and ellipse; sector area of ellipse between φ1 and φ2 equals (ab/2)(φ2 − φ1) (equation (17)), and segment formulae follow (equation (18)). These relations enable area computations and constructions by transferring to the circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of equal-area divisions and maximum-inscribed polygons via the auxiliary circle
rubrics_metrics.description: If a regular n-gon is inscribed in the auxiliary circle, dropping perpendiculars from its vertices to the ellipse divides the ellipse into n equal sectors and yields vertices of a maximum-area n-gon inscribed in the ellipse. There are indefinitely many such constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure (D): describe circle on major axis AB, inscribe regular polygon Q1...Qn, drop perpendiculars to AB meeting ellipse in P1...Pn; P1...Pn are vertices of equal sectors and of a maximal-area inscribed polygon. This depends on the ability to construct regular n-gons in the circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of maximum inscribed polygons
rubrics_metrics.description: A polygon inscribed in an ellipse is maximum (for fixed n) when the corresponding polygon in the auxiliary circle is regular; equivalently, at each vertex Pm the tangent is parallel to the chord P_{m−1}P_{m+1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use eccentric-anomaly relations: condition tan φ_m = tan(1/2(φ_{m−1}+φ_{m+1})) leads to identities showing regularity in the circle. The paper gives practical construction and multiple maxima exist because the circle's starting angle is arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum circumscribed polygons via tangents and locus of vertices
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimum-area polygon circumscribing the ellipse with n sides is obtained by taking tangents at the vertices P1...Pn of a maximal inscribed n-gon; the corresponding circumscribed polygon about the auxiliary circle is regular. The locus of angular points of all minimum circumscribing n-gons is a concentric similar ellipse with semiaxes a sec(π/n) and b sec(π/n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct P1...Pn as in the inscribed maximum case, then intersect tangents to obtain circumscribing polygon R1...Rn. The paper provides formulae for radii relations (e.g., p'_m = r'_m sec(π/n)) and area expressions for minimum circumscribed polygons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special properties for hexagon and quadrilateral cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A maximum hexagon inscribed in an ellipse has each side equal to the radius parallel to it (H). A minimum quadrilateral circumscribing an ellipse touches at extremities of conjugate diameters and is a parallelogram with sides equal and parallel to those diameters (R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are special cases derived from the general chord/radius relations (equations provided), useful as quick tests or constructions in these specific n values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangent plane to a surface of arbitrary order — procedure and formula
rubrics_metrics.description: For a surface given by homogeneous polynomial F(x,y,z)=0 of order ≤ n, the tangent plane at a point (x1,y1,z1) can be obtained by translating origin to that point, expanding with binomial theorem, and collecting linear terms; the general tangent-plane linear form is ax + by + cz = 0 with coefficients a,b,c determined by partial expansions (formula (13) and its detailed expanded form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the paper’s method: substitute x = x1 + X, etc., expand, drop higher than linear terms because the point lies on the surface, equate linear part to zero to get tangent plane. The provided explicit expression gives the coefficients for a general polynomial; when all linear-coefficient values vanish, the point is singular and tangents do not lie in one plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plane containing any two rectilinear tangents contains all tangents at that point
rubrics_metrics.description: At a non-singular point of a surface of finite order, any two rectilinear tangents determine a plane which contains every rectilinear tangent at that point; thus the locus of rectilinear tangents is a single plane (the tangent plane).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate by choosing coordinate planes, finding the three rectilinear tangents in coordinate traces and showing the plane containing two contains the third; this justifies the tangent-plane construction method and underlines the uniqueness of the tangent plane at a nonsingular point.
